authentication vs authorization: who you are vs what you may do

claims.claim: Authorization is the process of verifying that a requested action or service is approved for a specific entity.
Authorization is distinct from authentication, which is the process of verifying an entity's identity.
A user who has been authenticated is often not authorized to access every resource or perform every action the system allows.
Role-based access control (RBAC) employs predefined roles that carry specific sets of privileges, and subjects are assigned to those roles.
Attribute-based access control (ABAC) determines authorization by evaluating attributes of the subject, object, requested operations, and in some cases environment conditions against policy.
A role definition is a collection of permissions, typically actions such as read, write, and delete, and a scope is the set of resources the access applies to.
Least privilege means assigning users only the minimum privileges necessary to complete their job, and failing to enforce it can jeopardize the confidentiality of sensitive resources.
Broken access control was ranked as the most concerning web security vulnerability in OWASP's 2021 Top 10.
Applications should deny access by default and validate permissions on every request, because an attacker only needs one missed check.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Attribution of the working definition of authorization. OWASP's cheat sheet presents the definition (verifying that a requested action or service is approved for a specific entity) as quoted from NIST but does not name a specific NIST publication.
positions: Attribute the definition to NIST directly
Attribute it to OWASP's guidance, which itself quotes NIST
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the definition to OWASP's developer guidance and notes that OWASP quotes NIST; no specific NIST publication is cited for the definition, avoiding an unsupported citation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Access control model taxonomy. Some treatments of access control add discretionary access control (DAC) and mandatory access control (MAC) alongside RBAC and ABAC, while others name only RBAC and ABAC.
positions: Cover RBAC, ABAC, DAC, and MAC
Cover only RBAC and ABAC at literacy level
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson covers only RBAC and ABAC, matching the topic scope for a literacy-level lesson; the scope section records DAC/MAC as out of scope.

sourceRecords.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
sourceRecords.notes: Reused id from the phase-2 registry with an identical URL; read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: authorization defined (quoting NIST) as the process of verifying that a requested action or service is approved for a specific entity; authorization distinct from authentication (verifying an entity's identity); authenticated users often not authorized for every resource or action; enforce least privilege (minimum privileges necessary to complete the job; failure jeopardizes confidentiality of sensitive resources); deny by default; validate permissions on every request; broken access control ranked the most concerning web security vulnerability in OWASP's 2021 Top 10. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-162: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sourceRecords.notes: Read the PDF text layer (downloaded from nvlpubs.nist.gov, the official distribution host) on 2026-08-21. Supports: ABAC as a logical access control methodology in which authorization to perform a set of operations is determined by evaluating attributes associated with the subject, object, requested operations, and in some cases environment conditions against policy, rules, or relationships; RBAC as employing pre-defined roles that carry a specific set of privileges and to which subjects are assigned (Manager vs Analyst example). Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Supports: RBAC as managing who has access to Azure resources, what they can do with those resources, and at what scope; a role assignment consisting of security principal, role definition, and scope; a role definition as a collection of permissions listing actions such as read, write, and delete; scope as the set of resources the access applies to (management group, subscription, resource group, or resource). Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.
